title: Hydration adoption: the kernel adopts a server-rendered data-if root or data-each row instead of cloning its template (kemiller2002/limen#39)
proposedAddition: In src/kernel/browser-kernel.ts, #applyIf and #applyEach, on first mount only: if the element immediately after the anchor (for data-if) carries data-limen-if equal to the binding key, or an element in the list's position carries data-limen-key equal to the item's key (for data-each), bind that element in place instead of cloning the template, remove the marker, and apply the projection to it as usual. Elements the projection does not claim (a stale row, a section the first projection hides) are removed exactly as today, and each adoption or discard is reported through DiagnosticsSink as a deterministic hydration diagnostic. Two attributes become declared modifiers in architecture/core.json (bindingPrimitives.modifiers: data-limen-if, data-limen-key); the six primitives, the four families, the root exports and the concepts are unchanged. Estimated +20 to +35 handwritten Core lines (about 2-4%, under the 10% trigger), no new file, no new export.
invariantOrUseCase: projection-output: a page that already shows a projection's result should be adopted, not rebuilt, so focus, selection, scroll position, media playback and keyed DOM identity survive the moment the engine starts. Every server- or statically-rendered Limen page (#38) faces this on every load; without it the kernel removes nothing but duplicates every rendered section and row next to its server-rendered copy.
whyNotHtmlCss: The duplication happens inside the kernel's mount step; markup and styles cannot stop the kernel cloning a template.
whyNotEngineLibrary: The engine never sees DOM nodes, so it cannot tell the kernel which existing element is which row; and it must not, by the boundary rule.
whyNotCapabilityPack: A pack is reached through the Capability seam after the handshake, as an effect; mounting happens inside #applyScope during projection, which no pack can intercept. A pack would have to reimplement projection application, i.e. become a second kernel.
whyNotForma: Forma owns interaction and presentation primitives, not how the kernel applies a projection. (Forma was not consulted from this session: access was not granted.)
whyNotGovernedAdapter: An adapter hosts a third-party surface inside an element the kernel already manages; it has no part in mounting the kernel's own templates.
whyNotTooling: Hydration happens in production page loads, not in development or CI.
whyNotHostRenderer: This is the alternative weighed hardest. An optional hydration host can run before the kernel, but the kernel keeps its mounted nodes in private state (binding.mounted, binding.instances) and always clones; a host can only delete the rendered markup (recreating everything, which #39 forbids) or leave it (duplicating everything). Making mounting pluggable instead would add a Core extension point larger than the adoption itself. The host can still own everything else in #39: the bounded startup-event replay and the mismatch report.

consumerEvidence.consumer: The optional server and static renderer (#38)
consumerEvidence.evidence: src/renderer/render.ts writes data-limen-if and data-limen-key; test/browser/packs/renderer shows the markers in Chromium

consumerEvidence.consumer: A second, independent consumer is not yet shown
consumerEvidence.evidence: No application in this repository server-renders yet besides the #38 fixture; the product site (site/fsharp) renders client-side. For a budget-growth admission the two-consumer rule does not apply mechanically, but the owner should weigh this.

complexityDelta: Estimated, to be measured by npm run check:core-budget once implemented: handwritten Core lines +20 to +35 (922 -> about 950, +2 to +4%), handwritten normalized bytes of the same order, emitted Core gzip +200 to +400 bytes; root exports, export families, binding primitives (6), capability families (4), runtime dependencies (0) and concepts (7) unchanged; binding modifiers 1 -> 3.
compatibilityImpact: Additive. A page without markers behaves exactly as today; markers only appear in renderer output. A page with markers whose projection differs is corrected by the projection, as any projection corrects the DOM, and the difference is reported. No protocol or contract change, so no guest language or fingerprint change.
negativeBoundaryTests: test/core-boundary.test.ts continues to reject any undeclared data-* attribute read by Core (a third marker would fail), Core importing the renderer, and a new Core file; test/core-budget.test.ts holds the growth under review; the kernel tests would cover adoption of matching markup, keyed identity across adoption, discard of stale rows, and that a page without markers is untouched.
guestLanguageImpact: None: the contract, the fingerprint and every F#, C# and Rust binding are unchanged. Guest engines already produce the projection the renderer writes.
